User: How can you make sure your sound system is set up to deliver the best sound experience at a Super Bowl party?: Chances are you, your significant other, your parents, and at least half of your friends are looking for somewhere to watch the big game this Sunday. Before you look into which pubs have the biggest televisions, why not host your own party? You really don’t need to be a huge football buff throw a wicked party that people will enjoy just as much as the game. Here are few tips to make sure your party is as entertaining and crowd pleasing as the game itself.
Invite your guests in advance – Sounds like common sense but like I said, everyone is looking for somewhere to watch the game. So make sure you invite your guests in advance to ensure a good turnout and to make sure you can plan accordingly.
Food, food, and more food – Perhaps the most important part of a football party, besides the actual game. The Super Bowl is one of the biggest events for food consumption and trust me, your guests will expect to indulge regardless of where the party is held. Stick with some classics that you can prepare ahead of time, like chili and pulled pork, but also provide a mixture of finger foods that guests can munch on throughout the entire game. Check out our SUNSET® favorites for football inspired appetizers.
Pump up the volume – This is going to be a loud party, whether you want it to be or not. Make sure your sound system is set up to deliver the best sound experience you can. This will ensure that no play goes missed and will get your party in the spirit. If you really want your guests to feel like they’re at the game, give them some fun sound makers like thundersticks and cowbells (of course, at your discretion).
Place your bets– Part of the fun of watching the Super Bowl is placing bets on the game. Having guests bet on a variety of things like the final score, number of fumbles, length of the halftime show, etc. Will get your guests into the game and make it a far more interactive experience. Plus, if someone gets to leave the party with a prize AND bragging rights, you can bet they’ll be attending your party again next year.
Support the teams – Make sure you know what teams are competing so you can prepare your décor accordingly. Even something as simple as having plates and cups in the color-scheme of the two teams will amp up the atmosphere. The more themed décor you have, the better in my books.
By following these easy guidelines, your football party is sure to get everyone cheering – even the ones that are there for the commercials. Happy hosting!

- make sure you have enough seating for everyone, and consider setting up different viewing areas (inside and outside, for example) in case some guests want to chat or take a break from the game.
- have a variety of drinks available, including non-alcoholic options, and encourage your guests to stay hydrated.
- keep the party organized by having a schedule of the game, commercial breaks, and any other activities you have planned. This will also help you avoid missing any important moments.
- provide some entertainment during halftime or other breaks, like a trivia game, a mini football tournament, or even a dance contest. This will keep the energy high and allow your guests to socialize.
- don't forget to clean up after the party and thank your guests for coming. A simple gesture like a thank-you note or a small gift will go a long way in making them feel appreciated.

User: How can you make sure your sound system is set up to deliver the best sound experience at a Super Bowl party?: Chances are you, your significant other, your parents, and at least half of your friends are looking for somewhere to watch the big game this Sunday. Before you look into which pubs have the biggest televisions, why not host your own party? You really don’t need to be a huge football buff throw a wicked party that people will enjoy just as much as the game. Here are few tips to make sure your party is as entertaining and crowd pleasing as the game itself.
Invite your guests in advance – Sounds like common sense but like I said, everyone is looking for somewhere to watch the game. So make sure you invite your guests in advance to ensure a good turnout and to make sure you can plan accordingly.
Food, food, and more food – Perhaps the most important part of a football party, besides the actual game. The Super Bowl is one of the biggest events for food consumption and trust me, your guests will expect to indulge regardless of where the party is held. Stick with some classics that you can prepare ahead of time, like chili and pulled pork, but also provide a mixture of finger foods that guests can munch on throughout the entire game. Check out our SUNSET® favorites for football inspired appetizers.
Pump up the volume – This is going to be a loud party, whether you want it to be or not. Make sure your sound system is set up to deliver the best sound experience you can. This will ensure that no play goes missed and will get your party in the spirit. If you really want your guests to feel like they’re at the game, give them some fun sound makers like thundersticks and cowbells (of course, at your discretion).
Place your bets– Part of the fun of watching the Super Bowl is placing bets on the game. Having guests bet on a variety of things like the final score, number of fumbles, length of the halftime show, etc. Will get your guests into the game and make it a far more interactive experience. Plus, if someone gets to leave the party with a prize AND bragging rights, you can bet they’ll be attending your party again next year.
Support the teams – Make sure you know what teams are competing so you can prepare your décor accordingly. Even something as simple as having plates and cups in the color-scheme of the two teams will amp up the atmosphere. The more themed décor you have, the better in my books.
By following these easy guidelines, your football party is sure to get everyone cheering – even the ones that are there for the commercials. Happy hosting!

User: Losing is no fun. A losing streak is even worse. A 31-game losing streak? Well, that’s another thing altogether. In the case of the Tufts University Jumbos, it was an embarrassing reminder of a mountain they needed to climb in order to gain the respect of their peers. I had spent all of last season covering every game at home and on the road in the hopes that they would finally break the streak that had been haunting the program for so long. It was a long and frustrating season for everyone involved, myself included, but the team showed signs of improvement, keeping most of the games competitive. Of course, there’s no such thing as a moral victory in sports, especially with the longest active streak in college football on everyone’s mind. This season, however, there was a buzz in the air as Tufts was set to open the season against Hamilton, a NESCAC rival that gave up the last Tufts win all the way back in September 2010. Thanks to the access granted to me by head coach Jay Civetti, I was able to spend a few days with the team as they prepared for the season opener. As an institutional photographer, it’s my part of my job to highlight the program and to show off the hard work and dedication that these student-athletes put in to their sport that their classmates might not otherwise see or even be aware of. In this case, the pressure was apparent. Everyone knew what was at stake. Building on the foundations and work ethic they had set the previous year, the Jumbos stormed out to an early lead and never let go. When the game clock ticked down to zero, it was like a champagne cork going off, as the pressure that had been building up over the past 4 years finally let out. An effort well earned, no doubt. You can see a loose edit of my coverage below, and to see full team coverage, be sure to check out Tufts Athletics. When it comes to pro football, it’s pretty much a given that if I’m covering the game, the weather is going to be terrible. Last year, it was the playoff game against the Broncos in single-degree temperatures. The two times before then, when I was working for Sports Illustrated as an assistant, it was pouring rain and sleet. My streak of bad weather NFL games was kept intact when the San Francisco Chronicle gave me a call asking if I could cover 49ers’ visit to Gillette Stadium to take on the Patriots. With a wintry mix in the forecast, it had all the makings for terrible shooting conditions. Despite the weather-related challenges, we were treated to a game with plenty of action all around. When the Patriots went down 31-3 early in the third quarter, the team looked cooked. But Tom Brady being Tom Brady, that was anything but the case, as the Pats rallied to erase a 28-point deficit. It wasn’t enough, though, as the 49ers managed to pull off one final score to win it, 41-34. Much thanks to Luanne Dietz at the Chron for hooking me up with the job. I don’t get to shoot enough football these days, so it was definitely a treat! 12/16/12 – FOXBORO, Mass. – 49ers wide receiver Randy Moss hauls in a touchdown catch against the Patriots in the first quarter of their game at Gillette Stadium on Dec. 16, 2012. 12/16/12 – FOXBORO, Mass. – 49ers wide receiver Randy Moss, left, celebrates his first quarter touchdown against the Patriots with quarterback Colin Kaepernick, center, and tackle Joe Staley in their game at Gillette Stadium on Dec. 16, 2012. 12/16/12 – FOXBORO, Mass. – 49ers safety Donte Whitner and Patriots wide receiver Wes Welker dive for a fumble in the first quarter in their game at Gillette Stadium on Dec. 16, 2012. The fumble was overturned upon review. 12/16/12 – FOXBORO, Mass. – 49ers fans cheer on their team in the first quarter against the Patriots at Gillette Stadium on Dec. 16, 2012. The 49ers won, 41-34. 12/16/12 – FOXBORO, Mass. – 49ers running back Frank Gore gets tackled by Patriots linebacker Brandon Spikes in the first quarter in their game at Gillette Stadium on Dec. 16, 2012. 12/16/12 – FOXBORO, Mass. – Patriots wide receiver Brandon Lloyd gets tackled by 49ers cornerback Tarell Brown in the second quarter of their game at Gillette Stadium on Dec. 16, 2012. 12/16/12 – FOXBORO, Mass. – 49ers cornerback Carlos Rogers runs back an interception in the first quarter against the Patriots in their game at Gillette Stadium on Dec. 16, 2012. 12/16/12 – FOXBORO, Mass. – Patriots running back Danny Woodhead dives into the end zone for a touchdown ahead of the tackle from 49ers safety Dashon Goldson in the third quarter in the Patriots' 41-34 loss to the 49ers at Gillette Stadium on Dec. 16, 2012. 12/17/12 – FOXBORO, Mass. – 49ers wide receiver Michael Crabtree breaks a tackle from Patriots cornerback Kyle Arrington, scoring a touchdown on the play, in their game at Gillette Stadium on Dec. 16, 2012. The 49ers won, 41-34. 12/17/12 – FOXBORO, Mass. – 49ers defensive tackle Ray McDonald loses his helmet as he sacks Patriots quarterback Tom Brady in the fourth quarter of their game at Gillette Stadium on Dec. 16, 2012. The 49ers won, 41-34. Could you paraphrase the part about the photographer's coverage of the Patriots versus the 49ers game despite the challenging weather conditions?

Alex Stein loves watching football, playing football and betting on football. That last activity has emerged as his favorite over the years, and at times it has been a lucrative pastime. He just has one problem: The Dallas Cowboys.
“It kills my fantasy team, because I always draft the Cowboys,” Stein said. “I can’t bet on other players in the NFC East because I hate those guys.” Stein, 27, said he’s lost a lot of money because of his emotional investment in the Cowboys.
More From Credit.com: Can Gambling Hurt Your Credit Score?
“I’m down maybe 70 or 80K,” he said. He’s not sure exactly how much, but he’s at a net loss over his years of betting. Still, he loves it. He really, really loves it. His voice is full of excitement and happiness, even when he talks about losing thousands of dollars, because he’s still talking about football. Little else seems to matter. He’s in five fantasy football leagues (for the uninitiated, that means he has five rosters made up of players around the league, whose performances earn him points against his opponent’s roster), and he also bets on the head-to-head matches.
It may seem crazy how someone could lose so much money over fantasy matchups, but betting on football adds up. Some of Stein’s leagues require a $1,000 buy-in, and he bets on college football as well. He says his alma mater, LSU, usually makes up for a lot of the money he loses on the Cowboys.
Stein said he doesn’t have debt, but he also doesn’t keep detailed track of his finances. His work in reality TV (behind and in front of the camera), as well as his work as a bail bondsman and car salesman allows him a comfortable lifestyle, to say the least, he said.
More From Credit.com: How Much Debt is Too Much?
Stein is definitely on the extreme side, but he’s not alone when it comes tying finances with football.
Sloane T. Davis is a self-described sports junkie in Los Angeles who teams up with a friend for fantasy football strategy. They had played in leagues separately but wanted to join an expensive league a few years ago ($1,000 buy-in), so they pooled their resources.
They’ve been partners for about 5 years, and they’re currently in two leagues (the other league cost $500 to play, and in both leagues, they split buy-ins and winnings). “We are the reigning champions 3 years in a row,” Davis said of their performance in one league. The other: “Last year we came in second because Matt Forte couldn’t reach a 1-yard hashmark.” It was a huge let-down (a couple hundred dollars’ worth). Such is the life of sports fans.
Still, her winnings allow her to live the sports-fan life she loves. Not only does she set aside money for the next season of fantasy football, and she uses the rest to watch her favorite teams, the New York Jets and San Francisco Giants. If games are west of the Rocky Mountains, Davis goes.
Those rewards don’t come without work. She and her partner have daily conference calls and discuss roster choices for hours a day, but it makes her happy, and it has paid off. Overall, Meyer has won about $10,000 playing fantasy football.
Fantasy football even helped him pay off debt. When he graduated from college, he had some credit card debt, and he joined a big league at work. It cost $200, and a partner at the firm doubled the pot, so when he won, he ended up with $4,000. He used it to pay his debt.

Question/Instruction: What do architects mean by seeking a "wholeness" in their designs, and how is this different from the approach taken by architects in the past?

Given material: THE VERY IDEA OF a face lift goes against the grain of most architects' thinking. Their instincts lean much more toward all-out plastic surgery, reshaping the body to take on a whole different cast. That is, if they are willing to keep the old body at all. Throwing it out and starting from scratch probably gets closer to their way of doing things.
Architects, so the common wisdom goes, want to remake the world, or at least as much of it as they can get their hands on. It's been true enough in the past, but has become less and less so in the last decade, as the architectural profession has been forced to face twin realities: the growing preference in our society both for preserving older buildings and for renovating what we have, rather than starting over again. Renovation is usually, though not always, cheaper than new construction, which makes it especially appealing in an age of monetary constraints. So it is partly a matter of esthetics, partly economics and partly common sense that have brought us here. But we are clearly at a moment when few architects dare to treat a renovation project as if it were a blank slate.
A generation ago, architects were taught that their mission was to leave a mark, and often, the stronger the better. New buildings were designed to stand out from their surroundings; renovations of older ones were done so that no one could fail to see the difference between the original and the addition. Even architects whose careers began relatively recently tended to operate this way. Think, for example, of Michael Graves, the Princeton, N.J.-based architect who in the late 1960's and early 70's first came into public view through the striking modernist additions he put onto older houses (which led some colleagues to dub him the ''Cubist kitchen king''). The very point of Graves's additions was to stand apart from the houses to which they were attached. They were highly abstract objects, possessed of far more sophistication than the original houses, and their aloofness was part of the architectural message. ''You are common, but I am something much more special,'' the additions seemed to sneer at the houses.
The attitude of Graves's early years was hardly his alone. At the beginning of the 70's, the New York City firm of Mayers & Schiff designed an addition to an old clapboard farmhouse in Connecticut in the form of a two-story-high cedar and glass box. Lest there be any mistake about the transition from new to old, the box was set at a diagonal from the original house and wrapped around one of its corners, the new literally encasing the old.
Even Robert A. M. Stern, an architect whose career has soared in the last decade, largely due to his success in reproducing traditional architectural styles, nonetheless felt that he could not afford to let his own work disappear beside that of another architect. At least that is what one major addition he completed in 1981 would suggest. The house is a huge Georgian-style mansion in Llewelyn Park, N.J.; the addition, which contains an indoor pool, is best described as something of an English Baroque pleasure pavilion with a greenhouse roof. And while it picks up a few details from the original house, no one could say it blends in softly.
IT IS TEMPTING TO think of the whole issue in terms of ego, given how much, even today, our image of the architect is shaped by such fictitious characters as Howard Roark in the Ayn Rand novel ''The Fountainhead.'' Her architect-hero stands defiantly against bourgeois taste, and would sooner burn his T-square than design a building that took its cues from anyone else's. But for all we might want to see the architect as a romantic hero - for all architects might want to see themselves as such - the truth is that most architecture is shaped by the prevailing taste of an age.
As a matter of fact, ego has relatively little to do with it. Indeed, in recent years some of the biggest egos in architecture have begun to do some of the most restrained work. Kevin Roche, who gave us the monumental additions to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in the 70's - wings whose glass and limestone forms contrast sharply with the classical, older sections of the Met - recently designed an addition to the Jewish Museum on Fifth Avenue that is simply an exact reproduction of the museum's original French Gothic mansion. The addition, which will go into construction later this year, is conceived as if to blend new and old into a seamless whole.
Similarly, Romaldo Giurgola, a winner of the American Institute of Architects' highest award, has proposed adding to Louis I. Kahn's Kimbell Museum of Art in Fort Worth by literally extending its design at each end. That project hasn't been received as well as the Roche plan, largely because the Kimbell, unlike the Jewish Museum, is considered to be one of the great works of American architecture. Tampering with it at all, even by replicating the original, has been viewed by many critics as akin to adding a few strokes to a Caravaggio.
These two examples are extreme ones, of course. Precisely duplicating what has come before is hardly the only mode of the hour, particularly for public buildings. But it is being done more and more. And the fact that architects of Giurgola's stature, or Roche's, would consider replicating sections of older buildings tells us how much architectural values have changed.
In the last few years, there has been less hubris in architectural design, less of the arrogant certainty that we can do much better than the architects of earlier generations, and much less of the patronizing attitude toward tradition that for many architects was the motivation for breaking away from the old style when designing a renovation or addition. The original building was there first - a simple fact, but one that today has come to earn it a certain degree of respect. We do not condescend to Georgian or Tudor or Shingle Style houses the way we once did. And we are much more likely now to understand how good the average, traditionally styled American house built before 1940 really is. Architects today know better than to treat it with scorn.
MORE THAN INSISTENT originality, we seek a kind of wholeness now, a sense that a building is part of a larger continuity. And if that means the architect is going to be able to express his or her own design sensibility slightly less, we seem to feel that it is a fair trade-off. By the same token, an expanded or renovated house need not look merely like a bigger version of what was there before. But it should take its cues from the original building. Sometimes those cues can be interpreted literally; in other circumstances, it makes more sense to let the original building set a tone, a direction to which the second architect can respond. If architecture can be thought of as a conversation, the new architect entering the house doesn't need to repeat the words of the first architect - but he or she at least ought to be speaking the same language.
A couple of recent examples: In Larchmont, N.Y., in 1987, the architects Karen Bausman and Leslie Gill of Bausman-Gill Associates completed a two-story modernist addition to a tiny one-story stucco cottage. To have the extra space they wanted yet still preserve several valued trees on the small plot, the addition had to be two stories tall. Had it imitated the Arts and Crafts style of the cottage, it would have risked overwhelming the original building. But the finished addition appears neither to dominate the cottage nor to be incompatible with it. Bausman-Gill used the same material, stucco, as in the original building and similar steel casement windows, allowing the cottage to initiate the conversation, so to speak. The result is a deft marriage of old and new, the whole being both comfortable and visually richer than either section could be on its own.
Similarly, the San Francisco architect Mark Mack took a less literal direction in his addition to a rough-concrete modern house of the 60's, set high in the hills of Berkeley, Calif. Mack's own work has a blunt, almost primitive quality to it, which created a certain compatibility at the outset. But the addition, completed in 1988, stands out sharply from the original building: Its stucco walls are painted a rusty red with indigo-blue trim, and it reads as a powerful sculptural presence on its own. Still, it was not built to stand alone, and doesn't. The addition and the original house strengthen each other, forming a complex and vivid whole. (Mack considered a scheme that was more literally derived from the original house, and left it up to the clients to decide how assertive they wanted him to be. He was pleased with their decision; the other scheme, he felt, was too accommodating.) While the version that was built is hardly indifferent to the original building, it strikes out independently - yet in a way that relates continually to the original, engaging it in a vibrant architectural dialogue.
The conversation is quieter on Long Island, where David Hannaford Mitchell transformed a huge white clapboard farmhouse in Remsenburg into a rambling but vastly more genteel house. The changes Mitchell made are quite dramatic. He took a bland building and refined it, adding shutters, multipaned windows, a cornice and decks framed in subtly detailed latticework. Inside, the rooms were reorganized to flow gracefully into one another. The result, which was finished in 1987, is a lively and energetic composition that manages not to be overrefined or precious. The basic strength of the big old farmhouse is still there: It has been dressed up on the outside and opened up inside to just the right degree to bring out its architectural potential.
And so it is with all of the best renovations. They do not defy or sneer at the buildings to which they are appended, but support them. Sometimes buildings are supported best simply by being continued or extended, sometimes by being altered quite dramatically. The point is that whatever is done, it is the original building that sets the tone.

User: What are some innovative techniques in architecture for creating sustainable buildings?
Assistant: 1. Green roofs: One way to decrease a building's carbon footprint is to create green roofs. Vegetation, soil and other layers of vegetation are used to absorb heat and regulate the temperature of a building, reducing energy consumption used on cooling or heating.

2. Passive solar building design: Solar energy can be harnessed through the use of strategically placed window openings and organizing the space of the building to help retain solar energy.

3. Recycled building materials: Sustainable buildings can be built using renewable or recycled materials, such as bamboo or straw so that the structures are renewable resource-based and waste is minimized.

4. Building integration with water systems: Sustainable architects practice programs such as rooftop water harvesting, grey water, and black water systems to decrease the impact of a building on the local water supply.

5. Energy-efficient lighting: Lighting represents up to 40% of a building's total energy bill. Energy-efficient lighting solutions like sensors and LED lights can help lessen the dependence on electricity.

6. Smart home systems: Integrating smart home systems can help automate and optimize the energy use of a building.

7. Net-zero buildings: The use of solar, wind or geothermal energy sources and advanced insulation can help create buildings that generate as much energy as they consume – net-zero buildings.

8. Integrated landscape design: Integrated landscape design help reduce soil erosion, absorb waste water, and enhance stormwater management, all while providing a pleasing aesthetic element to a building's surrounding environment.

User: Here is a piece of text: THE VERY IDEA OF a face lift goes against the grain of most architects' thinking. Their instincts lean much more toward all-out plastic surgery, reshaping the body to take on a whole different cast. That is, if they are willing to keep the old body at all. Throwing it out and starting from scratch probably gets closer to their way of doing things.
Architects, so the common wisdom goes, want to remake the world, or at least as much of it as they can get their hands on. It's been true enough in the past, but has become less and less so in the last decade, as the architectural profession has been forced to face twin realities: the growing preference in our society both for preserving older buildings and for renovating what we have, rather than starting over again. Renovation is usually, though not always, cheaper than new construction, which makes it especially appealing in an age of monetary constraints. So it is partly a matter of esthetics, partly economics and partly common sense that have brought us here. But we are clearly at a moment when few architects dare to treat a renovation project as if it were a blank slate.
A generation ago, architects were taught that their mission was to leave a mark, and often, the stronger the better. New buildings were designed to stand out from their surroundings; renovations of older ones were done so that no one could fail to see the difference between the original and the addition. Even architects whose careers began relatively recently tended to operate this way. Think, for example, of Michael Graves, the Princeton, N.J.-based architect who in the late 1960's and early 70's first came into public view through the striking modernist additions he put onto older houses (which led some colleagues to dub him the ''Cubist kitchen king''). The very point of Graves's additions was to stand apart from the houses to which they were attached. They were highly abstract objects, possessed of far more sophistication than the original houses, and their aloofness was part of the architectural message. ''You are common, but I am something much more special,'' the additions seemed to sneer at the houses.
The attitude of Graves's early years was hardly his alone. At the beginning of the 70's, the New York City firm of Mayers & Schiff designed an addition to an old clapboard farmhouse in Connecticut in the form of a two-story-high cedar and glass box. Lest there be any mistake about the transition from new to old, the box was set at a diagonal from the original house and wrapped around one of its corners, the new literally encasing the old.
Even Robert A. M. Stern, an architect whose career has soared in the last decade, largely due to his success in reproducing traditional architectural styles, nonetheless felt that he could not afford to let his own work disappear beside that of another architect. At least that is what one major addition he completed in 1981 would suggest. The house is a huge Georgian-style mansion in Llewelyn Park, N.J.; the addition, which contains an indoor pool, is best described as something of an English Baroque pleasure pavilion with a greenhouse roof. And while it picks up a few details from the original house, no one could say it blends in softly.
IT IS TEMPTING TO think of the whole issue in terms of ego, given how much, even today, our image of the architect is shaped by such fictitious characters as Howard Roark in the Ayn Rand novel ''The Fountainhead.'' Her architect-hero stands defiantly against bourgeois taste, and would sooner burn his T-square than design a building that took its cues from anyone else's. But for all we might want to see the architect as a romantic hero - for all architects might want to see themselves as such - the truth is that most architecture is shaped by the prevailing taste of an age.
As a matter of fact, ego has relatively little to do with it. Indeed, in recent years some of the biggest egos in architecture have begun to do some of the most restrained work. Kevin Roche, who gave us the monumental additions to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in the 70's - wings whose glass and limestone forms contrast sharply with the classical, older sections of the Met - recently designed an addition to the Jewish Museum on Fifth Avenue that is simply an exact reproduction of the museum's original French Gothic mansion. The addition, which will go into construction later this year, is conceived as if to blend new and old into a seamless whole.
Similarly, Romaldo Giurgola, a winner of the American Institute of Architects' highest award, has proposed adding to Louis I. Kahn's Kimbell Museum of Art in Fort Worth by literally extending its design at each end. That project hasn't been received as well as the Roche plan, largely because the Kimbell, unlike the Jewish Museum, is considered to be one of the great works of American architecture. Tampering with it at all, even by replicating the original, has been viewed by many critics as akin to adding a few strokes to a Caravaggio.
These two examples are extreme ones, of course. Precisely duplicating what has come before is hardly the only mode of the hour, particularly for public buildings. But it is being done more and more. And the fact that architects of Giurgola's stature, or Roche's, would consider replicating sections of older buildings tells us how much architectural values have changed.
In the last few years, there has been less hubris in architectural design, less of the arrogant certainty that we can do much better than the architects of earlier generations, and much less of the patronizing attitude toward tradition that for many architects was the motivation for breaking away from the old style when designing a renovation or addition. The original building was there first - a simple fact, but one that today has come to earn it a certain degree of respect. We do not condescend to Georgian or Tudor or Shingle Style houses the way we once did. And we are much more likely now to understand how good the average, traditionally styled American house built before 1940 really is. Architects today know better than to treat it with scorn.
MORE THAN INSISTENT originality, we seek a kind of wholeness now, a sense that a building is part of a larger continuity. And if that means the architect is going to be able to express his or her own design sensibility slightly less, we seem to feel that it is a fair trade-off. By the same token, an expanded or renovated house need not look merely like a bigger version of what was there before. But it should take its cues from the original building. Sometimes those cues can be interpreted literally; in other circumstances, it makes more sense to let the original building set a tone, a direction to which the second architect can respond. If architecture can be thought of as a conversation, the new architect entering the house doesn't need to repeat the words of the first architect - but he or she at least ought to be speaking the same language.
A couple of recent examples: In Larchmont, N.Y., in 1987, the architects Karen Bausman and Leslie Gill of Bausman-Gill Associates completed a two-story modernist addition to a tiny one-story stucco cottage. To have the extra space they wanted yet still preserve several valued trees on the small plot, the addition had to be two stories tall. Had it imitated the Arts and Crafts style of the cottage, it would have risked overwhelming the original building. But the finished addition appears neither to dominate the cottage nor to be incompatible with it. Bausman-Gill used the same material, stucco, as in the original building and similar steel casement windows, allowing the cottage to initiate the conversation, so to speak. The result is a deft marriage of old and new, the whole being both comfortable and visually richer than either section could be on its own.
Similarly, the San Francisco architect Mark Mack took a less literal direction in his addition to a rough-concrete modern house of the 60's, set high in the hills of Berkeley, Calif. Mack's own work has a blunt, almost primitive quality to it, which created a certain compatibility at the outset. But the addition, completed in 1988, stands out sharply from the original building: Its stucco walls are painted a rusty red with indigo-blue trim, and it reads as a powerful sculptural presence on its own. Still, it was not built to stand alone, and doesn't. The addition and the original house strengthen each other, forming a complex and vivid whole. (Mack considered a scheme that was more literally derived from the original house, and left it up to the clients to decide how assertive they wanted him to be. He was pleased with their decision; the other scheme, he felt, was too accommodating.) While the version that was built is hardly indifferent to the original building, it strikes out independently - yet in a way that relates continually to the original, engaging it in a vibrant architectural dialogue.
The conversation is quieter on Long Island, where David Hannaford Mitchell transformed a huge white clapboard farmhouse in Remsenburg into a rambling but vastly more genteel house. The changes Mitchell made are quite dramatic. He took a bland building and refined it, adding shutters, multipaned windows, a cornice and decks framed in subtly detailed latticework. Inside, the rooms were reorganized to flow gracefully into one another. The result, which was finished in 1987, is a lively and energetic composition that manages not to be overrefined or precious. The basic strength of the big old farmhouse is still there: It has been dressed up on the outside and opened up inside to just the right degree to bring out its architectural potential.
And so it is with all of the best renovations. They do not defy or sneer at the buildings to which they are appended, but support them. Sometimes buildings are supported best simply by being continued or extended, sometimes by being altered quite dramatically. The point is that whatever is done, it is the original building that sets the tone.

2. Steven Holl Architects: The New York-based firm has distinguished itself by designing several additions to historic structures that preserve the original character while adding a modern twist. For example, their renovation of the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City preserves the museum's original Beaux-Arts style, while adding a series of glass pavilions that draw in natural light.

3. The restoration preserved the Beaux-Arts style of the original building while adding a new wing that connects the museum's three buildings.

4. Herzog & de Meuron: The Swiss architecture firm is known for its innovative approach to designing new buildings for existing sites. For example, its renovation of the Tate Modern museum in London transformed the former power station into a contemporary art museum that preserved the building's industrial feel while adding a sleek, modern twist.

Overall, there is a growing trend among architects to embrace the preservation and renovation of older buildings, rather than tearing them down and starting from scratch. User: What are some innovative techniques in architecture for creating sustainable buildings?
Assistant: 1. Green roofs: One way to decrease a building's carbon footprint is to create green roofs. Vegetation, soil and other layers of vegetation are used to absorb heat and regulate the temperature of a building, reducing energy consumption used on cooling or heating.

2. Passive solar building design: Solar energy can be harnessed through the use of strategically placed window openings and organizing the space of the building to help retain solar energy.

3. Recycled building materials: Sustainable buildings can be built using renewable or recycled materials, such as bamboo or straw so that the structures are renewable resource-based and waste is minimized.

4. Building integration with water systems: Sustainable architects practice programs such as rooftop water harvesting, grey water, and black water systems to decrease the impact of a building on the local water supply.

5. Energy-efficient lighting: Lighting represents up to 40% of a building's total energy bill. Energy-efficient lighting solutions like sensors and LED lights can help lessen the dependence on electricity.

6. Smart home systems: Integrating smart home systems can help automate and optimize the energy use of a building.

7. Net-zero buildings: The use of solar, wind or geothermal energy sources and advanced insulation can help create buildings that generate as much energy as they consume – net-zero buildings.

8. Integrated landscape design: Integrated landscape design help reduce soil erosion, absorb waste water, and enhance stormwater management, all while providing a pleasing aesthetic element to a building's surrounding environment.
User: Wow, these techniques are so impressive! Do sustainable buildings cost more to build than traditional ones?
Assistant: In the past, sustainable buildings had a reputation for being expensive to construct. However, with advancements in technology and sustainable design, the costs of sustainable building are becoming increasingly comparable to those of traditional homes or buildings. While some sustainable building techniques can still be more costly initially, they can result in significant savings over the long term through energy savings and operational efficiencies. Plus, as demand for sustainable buildings grows, economies of scale will make it easier and less expensive to incorporate sustainable features and building techniques into new and existing buildings.

Governments and non-profit organizations are offering incentives and certifications to encourage the construction of more sustainable buildings as well. All these efforts will go a long way towards creating a healthier and more sustainable future.

4. Grants and Rebates: Many states, municipalities, and utility companies offer grants and rebates to homeowners who incorporate sustainable building practices into their homes. These programs can help provide financial incentives to make sustainable building more accessible and affordable.

5. Green Building Programs: Many states have green building programs. For example, California's Green Building Standards Code (CALGreen) has been designed to help reduce greenhouse gas emissions and promote sustainable building practices.

These are just a few examples of the many certifications and incentives available for sustainable building practices. With a little research, you can find the ones that are most relevant to your location and construction goals.

Throwing it out and starting from scratch probably gets closer to their way of doing things.
Architects, so the common wisdom goes, want to remake the world, or at least as much of it as they can get their hands on. It's been true enough in the past, but has become less and less so in the last decade, as the architectural profession has been forced to face twin realities: the growing preference in our society both for preserving older buildings and for renovating what we have, rather than starting over again. Renovation is usually, though not always, cheaper than new construction, which makes it especially appealing in an age of monetary constraints. So it is partly a matter of esthetics, partly economics and partly common sense that have brought us here. But we are clearly at a moment when few architects dare to treat a renovation project as if it were a blank slate.
A generation ago, architects were taught that their mission was to leave a mark, and often, the stronger the better. New buildings were designed to stand out from their surroundings; renovations of older ones were done so that no one could fail to see the difference between the original and the addition. Even architects whose careers began relatively recently tended to operate this way. Think, for example, of Michael Graves, the Princeton, N.J.-based architect who in the late 1960's and early 70's first came into public view through the striking modernist additions he put onto older houses (which led some colleagues to dub him the ''Cubist kitchen king''). The very point of Graves's additions was to stand apart from the houses to which they were attached. They were highly abstract objects, possessed of far more sophistication than the original houses, and their aloofness was part of the architectural message. At the beginning of the 70's, the New York City firm of Mayers & Schiff designed an addition to an old clapboard farmhouse in Connecticut in the form of a two-story-high cedar and glass box. Lest there be any mistake about the transition from new to old, the box was set at a diagonal from the original house and wrapped around one of its corners, the new literally encasing the old.
Even Robert A. M. Stern, an architect whose career has soared in the last decade, largely due to his success in reproducing traditional architectural styles, nonetheless felt that he could not afford to let his own work disappear beside that of another architect. At least that is what one major addition he completed in 1981 would suggest. The house is a huge Georgian-style mansion in Llewelyn Park, N.J.; the addition, which contains an indoor pool, is best described as something of an English Baroque pleasure pavilion with a greenhouse roof. And while it picks up a few details from the original house, no one could say it blends in softly.
IT IS TEMPTING TO think of the whole issue in terms of ego, given how much, even today, our image of the architect is shaped by such fictitious characters as Howard Roark in the Ayn Rand novel ''The Fountainhead.'' Her architect-hero stands defiantly against bourgeois taste, and would sooner burn his T-square than design a building that took its cues from anyone else's. But for all we might want to see the architect as a romantic hero - for all architects might want to see themselves as such - the truth is that most architecture is shaped by the prevailing taste of an age.
As a matter of fact, ego has relatively little to do with it. Indeed, in recent years some of the biggest egos in architecture have begun to do some of the most restrained work. Kahn's Kimbell Museum of Art in Fort Worth by literally extending its design at each end. And the fact that architects of Giurgola's stature, or Roche's, would consider replicating sections of older buildings tells us how much architectural values have changed.

We do not condescend to Georgian or Tudor or Shingle Style houses the way we once did. Their instincts lean much more toward all-out plastic surgery, reshaping the body to take on a whole different cast. That is, if they are willing to keep the old body at all. Throwing it out and starting from scratch probably gets closer to their way of doing things.
Architects, so the common wisdom goes, want to remake the world, or at least as much of it as they can get their hands on. It's been true enough in the past, but has become less and less so in the last decade, as the architectural profession has been forced to face twin realities: the growing preference in our society both for preserving older buildings and for renovating what we have, rather than starting over again. Renovation is usually, though not always, cheaper than new construction, which makes it especially appealing in an age of monetary constraints. So it is partly a matter of esthetics, partly economics and partly common sense that have brought us here. But we are clearly at a moment when few architects dare to treat a renovation project as if it were a blank slate.
A generation ago, architects were taught that their mission was to leave a mark, and often, the stronger the better. New buildings were designed to stand out from their surroundings; renovations of older ones were done so that no one could fail to see the difference between the original and the addition. Even architects whose careers began relatively recently tended to operate this way. Think, for example, of Michael Graves, the Princeton, N.J.-based architect who in the late 1960's and early 70's first came into public view through the striking modernist additions he put onto older houses (which led some colleagues to dub him the ''Cubist kitchen king''). The very point of Graves's additions was to stand apart from the houses to which they were attached. They were highly abstract objects, possessed of far more sophistication than the original houses, and their aloofness was part of the architectural message. ''You are common, but I am something much more special,'' the additions seemed to sneer at the houses.
The attitude of Graves's early years was hardly his alone. At the beginning of the 70's, the New York City firm of Mayers & Schiff designed an addition to an old clapboard farmhouse in Connecticut in the form of a two-story-high cedar and glass box. Lest there be any mistake about the transition from new to old, the box was set at a diagonal from the original house and wrapped around one of its corners, the new literally encasing the old.
Even Robert A. M. Stern, an architect whose career has soared in the last decade, largely due to his success in reproducing traditional architectural styles, nonetheless felt that he could not afford to let his own work disappear beside that of another architect. At least that is what one major addition he completed in 1981 would suggest. The house is a huge Georgian-style mansion in Llewelyn Park, N.J.; the addition, which contains an indoor pool, is best described as something of an English Baroque pleasure pavilion with a greenhouse roof. And while it picks up a few details from the original house, no one could say it blends in softly.
IT IS TEMPTING TO think of the whole issue in terms of ego, given how much, even today, our image of the architect is shaped by such fictitious characters as Howard Roark in the Ayn Rand novel ''The Fountainhead.'' Her architect-hero stands defiantly against bourgeois taste, and would sooner burn his T-square than design a building that took its cues from anyone else's. But for all we might want to see the architect as a romantic hero - for all architects might want to see themselves as such - the truth is that most architecture is shaped by the prevailing taste of an age.
As a matter of fact, ego has relatively little to do with it. Indeed, in recent years some of the biggest egos in architecture have begun to do some of the most restrained work. Kevin Roche, who gave us the monumental additions to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in the 70's - wings whose glass and limestone forms contrast sharply with the classical, older sections of the Met - recently designed an addition to the Jewish Museum on Fifth Avenue that is simply an exact reproduction of the museum's original French Gothic mansion. The addition, which will go into construction later this year, is conceived as if to blend new and old into a seamless whole.
Similarly, Romaldo Giurgola, a winner of the American Institute of Architects' highest award, has proposed adding to Louis I. Kahn's Kimbell Museum of Art in Fort Worth by literally extending its design at each end. Tampering with it at all, even by replicating the original, has been viewed by many critics as akin to adding a few strokes to a Caravaggio.

We do not condescend to Georgian or Tudor or Shingle Style houses the way we once did. Sometimes those cues can be interpreted literally; in other circumstances, it makes more sense to let the original building set a tone, a direction to which the second architect can respond. If architecture can be thought of as a conversation, the new architect entering the house doesn't need to repeat the words of the first architect - but he or she at least ought to be speaking the same language.

Buildings are designed to reflect cultural values, and the aesthetic considerations can be highly symbolic. c55-m1.summary: The user is returning home after a long absence.
c55-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: It's good to be back home after so long.
Assistant: How does it feel to be back in your childhood home?
User: Nostalgic, I guess. It brings back a lot of memories.
Assistant: Yeah, I can imagine. Do you think anything has changed?
User: Not really, everything is pretty much the same as I remember it.
Assistant: That's cool. Have you visited any old hangouts or places you used to frequent?
User: Yeah, I went to my old high school and drove by some of the parks we used to go to.
Assistant: Did it all feel familiar?
User: Yeah, it did. It's weird how even after so many years, these places can still feel the same.
Assistant: It's like they have a sense of permanence, right?
User: Exactly. It's good to be back, though. I missed this place.
Assistant: I bet. I'm glad you're enjoying your trip back home.
User: I was just staring up at the planes in the sky and it made me feel so nostalgic.
Assistant: Nostalgic? Why is that?
User: I just remember all the times I used to travel on those planes to different parts of the country. It was such an exciting feeling being up in the air and looking down at the world below me.
Assistant: That sounds amazing. I've always wanted to travel by plane, but I'm too scared to do it.
User: Oh, you shouldn't be! It's such a safe mode of transportation. Plus, the feeling of taking off and landing is completely exhilarating.
Assistant: I don't know, I feel like I would be so nervous the entire time. But I do understand the nostalgia aspect. Looking back on memories of traveling can be so heartwarming.
User: Definitely. And it's something I want to continue doing in the future, once it's safe to travel again. But for now, I'm just going to keep staring up at those planes and reminiscing about my past travels.
Assistant: That's a great idea. And hey, maybe someday I'll summon up the courage to hop on one of those planes too.

User: Analyze the impact of nostalgia on the entertainment industry and identify potential opportunities for leveraging this trend.
Assistant: Nostalgia has become a major trend in the entertainment industry in recent years. It refers to the sentimental longing or affection for a past time or era, and it is a powerful tool that can be used to connect with audiences and evoke emotions. The impact of nostalgia on the entertainment industry can be seen in many different areas such as music, movies, television shows, and even video games. Here are some potential opportunities for leveraging this trend:

1. Reviving old franchises: Many entertainment companies have realized the potential of nostalgia and are now reviving old franchises such as Star Wars, Ghostbusters, and Jurassic Park, to name a few. These revivals have proven to be successful at the box office, especially with audiences who were fans of the original franchise. By bringing back beloved characters and stories, companies can tap into the nostalgia of the audience and create new revenue streams.

2. Developing new content that pays homage to the past: Another way to leverage nostalgia is by developing new content that pays homage to the past. This could be in the form of period dramas, music that pays tribute to a certain era or sound, or movies that are inspired by classic films. By taking inspiration from the past while still creating something new, companies can appeal to both a new audience and a fan base that is already familiar with the material.

3. Creating experiences that transport people back in time: Nostalgia can also be used to create experiences that transport people back in time. This could be in the form of themed restaurants, nostalgic theme parks, or interactive exhibits that allow people to relive their favorite memories. These experiences allow people to connect with their past in a fun and immersive way.

4. Using social media to tap into nostalgia: Finally, social media platforms like Instagram and TikTok have become a powerful tool for tapping into nostalgia. Brands and influencers can use these platforms to share images and videos that celebrate the past and evoke feelings of nostalgia. By tapping into the collective memories of their audience, companies can build deeper connections with their fans and drive engagement.

In conclusion, nostalgia is a powerful tool that can be leveraged by the entertainment industry in many different ways. By reviving old franchises, developing new content that pays homage to the past, creating experiences that transport people back in time, and using social media to tap into nostalgia, companies can tap into the emotional connection that audiences have with their past and create new opportunities for growth and engagement.

We were crammed in there like sardines, but I remember feeling so happy and content just being together. As I reflect on my childhood, I realize how much it shaped the person I am today. My experiences taught me the values of family, resilience, identity, and growth. As I continue to grow and change, I carry these experiences with me, grateful for the lessons they taught me.

Assistant: Growing up, my childhood was a battlefield. My parents had divorced when I was only six years old, and that moment in my life became my personal catalyst for overcoming adversity.

The first few years after the divorce were filled with chaos and uncertainty. I moved around a lot, shuttled between my mother and father's homes. During that time, I often felt like a piece of luggage being lugged from one place to another. It was tough to feel settled and secure, unable to gain any sense of stability or foundation.

The transition wasn't just about navigating physical changes, though. My parents' marriage had ended bitterly, and that left deep emotional scars for everyone involved. Both my mother and father struggled with their own demons, and the fallout from the divorce further fueled their sense of anger and resentment.

Growing up, I often found myself caught in the crossfire of my parents' battles. They would argue and storm off, leaving me with a constant sense of unease and not knowing what to think or feel.

The turning point came when I was 12 years old. At that age, I had been struggling at school for some time. My grades were poor, and I had little interest in learning or pursuing academics. I felt like I was slipping through the cracks and that the future wasn't looking too bright. But then, something amazing happened.

I met a teacher who made a tremendous impact on my life. Ms. Johnson saw something in me that I didn't even know existed - she believed in me. She saw potential, possibility and the chance for me to achieve great things. She took me under her wing, became a mentor and began to teach me how to overcome my difficulties.

At first, I was resistant to her approach. I was guarded and skeptical of anyone wanting to help me navigate the challenges of life. But Ms. Johnson's persistence and unwavering belief in me transformed my outlook on life. She showed me that I wasn't just a product of my upbringing or my environment, but that I had the power to shape my own destiny.

Through her guidance, I learned that resilience, inner strength and personal growth could make all the difference. I started to believe in myself more and began to take small steps to better myself.

One of the essential lessons I learned is that life is full of challenges and obstacles, but it's not the challenges themselves that define us. It's how we respond to them that determines our character and ultimately our destiny.

Another critical moment in my journey came when I was 18 years old. I landed a job working at a summer camp for kids who had gone through traumatic experiences. I saw so many parallels between the struggles that these kids faced and my own experiences growing up. It was an incredibly cathartic and transformative experience, giving me the chance to give back to others by sharing my own journey.

Looking back on my journey, I realized that everything that happened in my life was leading me to where I am today. While it was tough and painful at times, those experiences sparked something within me that helped me become the person that I am today.

My experiences taught me that it's easy to get knocked down by life, but the only way to truly fail is to give up. Resilience, determination, and the willingness to learn and grow are the keys to overcoming adversity, not just surviving but thriving.

Today, I am proud of the person I've become. I still face challenges and obstacles, but I've also developed the tools and mindset to overcome them effectively. It's an ongoing journey of self-discovery, but I'm grateful for everything that's led me to where I am today.

Assistant: That can be frustrating when you're trying to understand someone's perspective. Do you think you'll try to bring it up again and ask them more about their thoughts on beauty contests?

User: There are moments when deep in thought or crazy in love that we forget how visible we are. We create a space that is undeniably our own. We don’t think about who can see us nor do we care. We simply love and exist.
On my drive into work the other day, I looked up at my rearview mirror and happened on a moment so private I couldn’t look away. A young couple on their way to school (I assume), were parked behind me at a red light. He was in the driver’s seat, staring at her like she was the most beautiful girl he’d ever seen. She looked upset, her blonde pigtail beneath a baseball cap swayed as she shook her head.
He smiled at her and reached his hand toward her face. He let it rest there until she lifted her own hand to hold it. A hint of a smile reached her lips as she turned her head and kissed his hand; then leaned over and kissed his cheek, once, twice, a third time for luck.
As I placed my coffee back in its holder I realized that I was still driving. The light blared green and I stepped on the gas in the hope that the young couple wouldn’t start honking me. I looked up every once in a while to see if they were still behind me. For a little while they were, smiling and laughing in their own little bubble. I lost them at some point but couldn’t seem to shake them from my mind.
I focus on the negative things in life. The days and weeks where everything goes wrong and the world appears to be a heaping pile of crap tend to weigh me down. I don’t think often enough about the many beautiful moments filled with love that I’ve witnessed or experienced. I guess sometimes all you need is a glance at your rearview mirror to remind you of how important those moments are. User: Can you provide tips on how to ensure that your written articles are engaging and interesting for readers?
Generate according to: Writing articles is a very basic, and integral, part of UK content marketing. But not all writing is good writing. Some are boring, and unworthy of reading at all. So how do you make sure your articles are not one of those?
Assistant: 1. Know your target audience: To ensure that your articles are engaging and interesting, you must first know your target audience. Understand their interests, needs, and pain points. This knowledge will enable you to write articles that appeal to them and provide relevant information.

2. Create a catchy headline: A headline is the first thing that readers see, and it can make or break your article. Therefore, create a catchy headline that intrigues readers and makes them want to read more.

3. Use an active voice: Using an active voice is not only more engaging, but it also makes your article easier to read. Write in a conversational tone to make the reader feel like they are having a conversation with you.

4. Avoid jargon: Unless you are writing for a specific audience that understands the terms, avoid using jargon. Use simple and understandable language that all readers can understand.

5. Add visuals: Images, videos, and infographics help to break up the text and make it more engaging. Use visuals to illustrate your points and make your article more appealing.

6. Tell a story: People love stories, and incorporating a narrative into your article will make it more interesting. Use anecdotes or real-life examples to bring your point home.

7. Provide value: Ensure that your article provides value to the reader. Whether it is informative or entertaining, ensure that the reader leaves with something they did not know before.

8. End with a call to action: A call to action encourages readers to engage with your content, whether it is through sharing, commenting or subscribing. End your article with a call to action that keeps readers engaged with your content.

User: Read the passage below and answer the question or follow the instruction: How does Patch's traffic and revenue compare to its number of employees? Passage: Patch is one of AOL CEO Tim Armstrong's biggest bets in his bid to save the company. So far, it has been a big waste of money. Patch employs about a 1,000 journalists and a couple hundred sales people. Meanwhile, Patch's 900 or so sites don't get enough traffic - about 10 million people visit the site each month - to bring in much advertising money. According to documents we've obtained from a source, Patch lost at least $100 million last year and generated paltry revenues. But as bad as Patch's cost structure is, it turns out Armstrong's big investment does, at least, have one very important thing going for it. The product is pretty good. I've learned this from a trusted though admittedly anecdotal source: my dad. Back in November, I was down in Florida visiting my family for Thanksgiving. We got to talking about how the local paper, The St. Petersburg Times, was changing its name to The Tampa Bay Times. We talked about new media startups like Business Insider are disrupting old media companies. The conversation changed to Patch somehow, and I had the idea to sign my Dad up for a daily email from a local Patch site. My dad does most of his business in downtown St. Petersburg, so I signed him up for the Patch about that area's closest neighborhood - call Old Northeast. I forgot all about the experiment until last weekend, when during a family get together, my dad spontaneously brought it up, saying: "I love that Patch thing you subscribed me to!" He told me that the emails have him considering canceling his subscription to The Tampa Bay Times. He's "almost" there. That's pretty remarkable, considering The Tampa Bay Times is, in media circles, considered one of the country's best regional papers. My dad says he only actually opens the Patch emails about three times a week (they come every day). He says he only actually clicks on stories in those emails maybe twice a week. What he likes about Patch's stories are that they are "timely" and "really local." The only thing that's really keeping him from pulling the trigger? "Significantly better sports coverage.That would kill the paper!" Confessions Of Patch Salesperson: "It's Been A Disaster"
